reason: The sources provide over 15 consistent claims from multiple distinct sites regarding its discovery, dimensions, and the scientific challenge it posed to cosmic models.
story: In 1989, astronomers Margaret Geller and John Huchra unveiled the CfA2 Great Wall, a structure so massive it shouldn't have existed. Using a 60-inch telescope in Arizona, they mapped the universe in 3D, revealing a colossal sheet of galaxies over 500 million light-years long. At the time, it was the largest structure ever seen. Its scale was a shock: under the standard Big Bang model, there simply hadn't been enough time in cosmic history for gravity to pull that much matter together. To explain it, scientists had to rely on dark matter—an invisible web acting as a gravitational skeleton for the stars. Even today, the Wall's true size is a mystery. Because it sits behind the thick dust and gas of our own Milky Way, in a region called the Zone of Avoidance, we cannot see where this cosmic giant actually ends.
angle: The Great Wall is so massive that the 13.8 billion years since the Big Bang shouldn't have been enough time for gravity to build it.

claims.claim: The CfA2 Great Wall was discovered in 1989.
The structure was discovered by American astronomers Margaret Geller and John Huchra.
It was discovered using data from the CfA Redshift Survey.
At the time of its discovery, it was the largest known structure in the universe.
The Great Wall is a colossal galaxy filament or sheet.
The structure is approximately 500 million light-years long.
The wall is located approximately 200 million light-years away from Earth.
The Great Wall cannot be seen with the unaided eye.
The structure was revealed through three-dimensional mapping using redshifts.
Data was gathered using the 60-inch telescope at the Whipple Observatory in Arizona.
The universe's large-scale structure resembles giant soap bubbles with galaxies on the 'skin.'
The Milky Way's dust and gas block the view of the Great Wall's true extent.
The region where the Milky Way obscures the view is known as the Zone of Avoidance.
Such large structures are difficult to explain within the timeframe since the Big Bang.
Dark matter is theorized to provide the gravity needed to form these superstructures.
Visible galaxies appear to pepper the dark matter structure like snow on mountaintops.
The Coma Cluster is a dense central region within the Great Wall.
The Great Wall is about 15 million light-years thick.

disputed: The exact width of the filament is reported as 200 million light-years by S2, 250 million by S3, and 300 million by S1, S4, and S5; the script should say 'hundreds of millions of light-years wide.'
The length is cited as 500 million light-years in most sources, but S3 states 600 million; the script should use 'over 500 million.'
S3 suggests the thickness is 30 million light-years, while all other sources state 15 million; attribute the larger figure to 'some measurements.'
